drills.q: Name the 5 GoF creational patterns and which language feature each was mostly a workaround for.
drills.a: Singleton (no first-class module state), Factory Method (no first-class functions), Abstract Factory (no interfaces for coherent product families), Builder (no keyword arguments), Prototype (no generic copy protocol). All are C++/Smalltalk-era workarounds per Norvig's 1996 analysis.

drills.q: Why is a class-based Singleton considered an anti-pattern today, and what's the fix?
drills.a: It hides global mutable state behind a private constructor, breaking test isolation and risking races, and structurally prevents 2 coexisting instances. Fix: a DI container's singleton scope or a cached provider function (@lru_cache, sync.Once) — the single-instance decision lives in the wiring layer, not the class.

drills.q: Distinguish Factory Method from Abstract Factory with a concrete example of when you'd upgrade one to the other.
drills.a: Factory Method dispatches to produce ONE product type. Abstract Factory bundles multiple factory methods to produce a coherent FAMILY. Upgrade example: you start with create_document(kind), then add create_exporter(kind) that must match the document's format — bundling both under one factory interface prevents mismatching a PDF document with an HTML exporter.

drills.q: Explain why Java needs a fluent Builder class but Python and Go typically don't, and name each language's actual idiom.
drills.a: Java lacks keyword arguments, so optional-heavy constructors become unreadable telescoping calls, hence a staged .builder().build() class. Python has keyword args + defaults, so a validating dataclass/Pydantic model does the job. Go has neither keyword args nor classic inheritance, so it uses functional options: variadic ...Option function parameters that mutate the struct being built.

drills.q: A team has an AbstractDatabaseFactory with a single PostgresFactory implementation and a comment 'add MySQL later.' Diagnose and recommend.
drills.a: Speculative generality / YAGNI violation: the abstraction cost (extra indirection, an interface to maintain) is being paid before a second implementation exists to justify it. Recommend collapsing to a plain PostgresConnection constructor now, reintroducing Abstract Factory only when a second real backend is scheduled work — unless the interface exists purely for test-fake substitution, which is a separate, valid justification.

drills.q: What's broken about Java's Cloneable interface, and what do production Java codebases use instead?
drills.a: Object.clone() is protected, performs only a shallow copy by default, can throw a checked CloneNotSupportedException even when cloning is always supported, and doesn't compose with generics or final fields. Production code typically uses a copy constructor or a static factory method like Config.copyOf(other) with explicit deep-copy logic.

drills.q: State Peter Norvig's 1996 argument about GoF patterns and evaluate whether it fully applies to all 23 patterns.
drills.a: Norvig argued ~16/23 GoF patterns vanish or become trivial in a language with first-class functions, closures, and multiple dispatch, since most patterns compensate for C++/Smalltalk's missing features. It's substantially right for creational patterns (Factory Method, Builder, Prototype collapse easily) but less complete for patterns whose value is structural coordination rather than missing syntax, e.g. Abstract Factory's family-coherence guarantee, or Observer/Iterator in the other GoF categories.

drills.q: Design the object-construction strategy for a multi-tenant SaaS backend needing a different storage backend (S3, Azure Blob, local disk) per tenant, chosen at request time. Explain where a naive Singleton would break this.
drills.a: Use Abstract Factory keyed by tenant config (StorageFactory interface with S3Factory/AzureFactory/LocalFactory), resolved per request or cached per tenant — not a process-wide Singleton, since Singleton allows only one instance per process and the requirement is multiple coexisting instances. Construction params (bucket, creds, region) flow through a validating config object (dataclass/Pydantic, the Builder's job) so malformed tenant config fails fast at construction. A naive StorageClient.getInstance() Singleton would immediately break this because it can only ever bind to one backend for the whole process.

drills.q: Why is Prototype risky for objects that hold live connections or other side-effecting resources?
drills.a: Cloning (deepcopy or a clone constructor) copies the reference/handle to the resource rather than establishing a fresh one, so two logical objects end up sharing one underlying socket or connection — violating the assumption that a clone is an independent, safely-mutable copy. Prototype is safe for pure-data templates, not for objects wrapping I/O handles.
